newsitem.title: USA: Oil prices fall, coffee at eight-month high.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices fall, coffee at eight-month high.

text.p: Oil prices fell Thursday as concerns about winter supplies of heating oil eased, while coffee prices roared to the highest levels in eight months.
Heating oil fell despite forecasts of much colder weather in the Northeast as supplies were now seen as sufficient for the winter.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, heating oil prices led the energy markets lower. February heating oil closed down 1.50 cents a gallon at 69.92 cents.
"There is talk of a lot of heating oil still coming up in the Colonial Pipeline," said Ed Kevelson, director of refined products for Paribas Futures Inc. in New York.

Colonial Pipeline Co., a major artery for energy to the East Coast, said it will continue rationing space on a huge pipeline through February because it still faced more demand than its 960,000 barrel-per-day line could handle.
The line runs from Houston to Greensboro, N.C., where it branches off to New York Harbour.
Meteorologists said temperatures will fall 10 to 20 degrees below normal this weekend in the Northeast, the largest heating oil market in the world.
But dealers said supply was now sufficient to cover winter demand after being historically low in the summer and fall.

According to the American Petroleum Institute's stocks report for the week ended Jan. 10, the year-to-year shortfall in stocks of distillates, which include heating oil and diesel fuel, has narrowed to 350,000 barrels from almost 20 million barrels last August.
"Heat's fall was also partly a function of traders selling it to buy gasoline since February gasoline spreads really firmed this time last year," said Kevelson.
February gasoline ended only 0.16 cent a gallon lower at 68.69 cents, while February crude oil closed down 43 cents a barrel at $25.52.

At New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, speculators shook off some bearish news and pushed the March coffee contract up to an eight-month high. March coffee closed up 0.45 cent per pound at 123.05 cents, its highest settlement since May 16.

The Green Coffee Association of New York reported that supplies of green coffee in U.S. warehouses rose in December by 63,000 132-pound bags to 1.327 million bags. Traders had expected a rise between 50,000 and 100,000 bags.
That supply rise, and news that dock workers in No. 2 coffee exporter Colombia ended a two-day strike, spurred some short-lived selling in futures. But it didn't last.
"The trend is turning and heading higher even though it is due for a correction," Allendale Inc. analyst Jim Cordier said. "It should be well supported near the highs."

At the Chicago Board of Trade, January soybeans closed 3 cents a bushel higher at $7.47-1/2 as speculators and commercial firms bought late in the day on concerns about the young Brazilian crop, currently struggling with hot summer weather.
"We've had enormous gains of late, and the bears have been trying to break the market but with very little success," said Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter.
March corn closed 1/4 cent a bushel lower at $2.73-1/2 as farmers' sales of cash corn picked up, fuelling hedge sales of futures contracts, floor traders said.
